latent_mechanisms.display_name: Ascending uropathogen colonization of upper urinary tract
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Periurethral/bladder uropathogens (predominantly E. coli with adhesins/P-fimbriae, also Klebsiella, Proteus, Enterococcus) ascend via the ureter to colonize the renal pelvis and calyces; this is the gateway mechanism that initiates pyelonephritis.

Active replication of uropathogens within renal pelvis, calyces, and tubules; the proximal mechanism that scales with bacteriuria, urinary nitrite/LE positivity, and urine culture CFU. Targeted directly by appropriate antimicrobial therapy.
Acute inflammation of the renal pelvis and calyceal urothelium; drives flank pain, CVA tenderness, pyuria, and white-cell casts.
Neutrophil-rich tubulointerstitial inflammation of the renal parenchyma, producing wedge-shaped hypoperfusion / striated nephrogram and tubular dysfunction; substrate for microabscess formation.
Neutrophil recruitment into renal cortex/medulla; pathologic substrate of acute pyelonephritis and feeder for microabscess and macroabscess formation.
Coalescence of neutrophilic infiltrates into multiple small (<1 cm) parenchymal microabscesses; precursor to macroscopic intrarenal abscess.
Coalescent suppurative cavity within the renal parenchyma (≥1 cm); often manifests as persistent fever despite appropriate antibiotics and may require drainage if >3–5 cm.

Extension of intrarenal suppuration through the renal capsule into the perinephric (Gerota's) space; classically presents with persistent fever and pain after several days of appropriate antibiotics and almost always requires drainage.

Mechanical obstruction (stone, stricture, tumor, extrinsic mass, congenital, sloughed papilla) creates retrograde pressure and stasis, sustaining pathogen proliferation and converting pyelonephritis into obstructive pyelonephritis / pyonephrosis — a urologic emergency requiring urgent decompression.
Hematogenous spread of uropathogens (positive in roughly 20–30% of hospitalized acute pyelonephritis) driving systemic endotoxin exposure and systemic inflammatory response.

LPS-triggered TLR4 activation with TNF/IL-1/IL-6 cascade producing fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, leukocytosis with left shift, CRP/procalcitonin elevation; intensity tracks with bacteremia and source-control adequacy.

Sepsis physiology with distributive shock, lactic acidosis, encephalopathy, coagulopathy, and AKI driven by gram-negative urosepsis; central determinant of short-term mortality and need for vasopressor/ICU support.

Multifactorial AKI: sepsis-related ATN (most common), direct tubulointerstitial injury, post-renal obstruction, and drug-related (aminoglycoside, contrast). Reversible if obstruction is relieved and sepsis is controlled.

Necrotizing renal infection with intraparenchymal/perinephric gas, almost exclusively in poorly controlled diabetes (with or without obstruction); high mortality. Huang–Tseng classification grades extent and guides percutaneous drainage vs nephrectomy.

Ischemic and infectious necrosis of renal papillae, classically in diabetes, sickle cell disease, NSAID/analgesic abuse, and urinary obstruction; can shed sloughed papillae causing secondary obstruction.

Activity of resistant organisms (ESBL Enterobacterales, AmpC, fluoroquinolone-resistant E. coli, occasional CRE, vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus) that defeat common empiric regimens and demand broader/definitive coverage.

Persistent unrelieved obstruction, undrained abscess, infected stone, infected stent/catheter, or necrotic tissue that perpetuates pathogen burden despite appropriate antibiotics; the dominant cause of clinical non-response after 48–72 h.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Ascending colonization of pelvis/calyces is the upstream prerequisite for upper-tract pathogen replication.
Active pathogen replication within renal pelvis triggers acute mucosal inflammation.
Inflammation extends from pyelocaliceal mucosa into adjacent medullary tubulointerstitium via collecting ducts.
Tubulointerstitial inflammation recruits neutrophils into cortex and medulla.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Worsened by source-control failure or initial inactive antibiotic exposure.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Coalescing neutrophilic foci form sub-centimeter parenchymal microabscesses.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Probability rises sharply when adequate antibiotics or drainage are delayed beyond 48–72 hours.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Microabscesses coalesce into ≥1 cm intrarenal abscess; classic cause of fever persisting past day 3 of effective antibiotics.
Untreated parenchymal abscess ruptures through the renal capsule into Gerota's fascia.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Risk amplified by obstruction, immunosuppression, diabetes, and intraparenchymal disease.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Heavy pyelocaliceal/parenchymal infection seeds the bloodstream via inflamed peritubular capillaries.
Circulating LPS triggers TLR4-mediated cytokine release.
Even without overt bacteremia, parenchymal infection drives systemic cytokine response.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Strongly amplified by obstruction, source-control failure, age >65, immunosuppression, diabetes.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Sustained cytokine activation produces distributive shock, AKI, encephalopathy, and coagulopathy.
Stasis above an obstruction creates a closed reservoir for unchecked bacterial replication; antibiotic penetration into pus/obstructed urine is poor.
Pyelovenous and pyelolymphatic backflow under obstructed pressure delivers organisms directly to the bloodstream.
Post-renal obstruction reduces GFR through elevated tubular pressure; bilateral or solitary-kidney obstruction is the dominant AKI driver.
Undrained abscess/pus, retained infected stones, or unaddressed obstruction sustain pathogen replication despite antibiotics.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Requires uncontrolled diabetes (>90% of cases) and frequently obstruction; gas-forming organisms (E. coli, Klebsiella) ferment glucose in necrotic tissue.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Substrate-rich diabetic medullary tissue plus impaired host defenses permit gas-forming necrotizing infection.
Necrotizing infection produces fulminant septic physiology and organ failure.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Conditional on initial empiric antibiotic failing to cover the organism.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Resistant organisms continue replicating under inactive empiric therapy, prolonging burden and bacteremia risk.
Sepsis-associated AKI from hypoperfusion, microvascular dysfunction, and inflammatory tubular injury.
Distension and inflammation of the renal capsule produce costovertebral angle tenderness on percussion.
Capsular stretch and pelvic inflammation produce unilateral (occasionally bilateral) flank pain.
Inflammatory exudate from pyelocaliceal mucosa releases neutrophils into urine.
WBC casts form when neutrophils are entrained in tubular Tamm–Horsfall protein matrix; nearly pathognomonic of upper-tract infection.
Wedge-shaped delayed enhancement on contrast CT/MRI reflects focal tubular obstruction and edema in inflamed parenchyma.
Capsular and perinephric edema from active parenchymal inflammation visible on CT.
Urothelial edema appears as concentric pelvicalyceal wall thickening on CT/US.
Upper-tract bacterial burden produces midstream/catheter urine culture growth (typically ≥10^5 CFU/mL, often ≥10^4 in catheter specimens).
Culture positivity directly reflects upper-tract pathogen replication unless masked by prior antibiotic exposure.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Falsely negative for non-nitrate-reducing organisms (Enterococcus, Staphylococcus saprophyticus, Pseudomonas) and dilute urine.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Enterobacterales reduce urinary nitrate to nitrite.
Surrogate marker for pyuria from any pathogen.
Most uropathogens are gram-negative bacilli (E. coli predominant).
The pyelocaliceal/parenchymal compartment is the urinary source of infection.
Direct readout of bacteremia.
Higher inoculum correlates with severity and shock risk.
Direct mapping; pyelonephritis is the leading source of community-acquired gram-negative bacteremia.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Blunted in elderly, immunocompromised, end-stage renal disease.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: IL-1/IL-6/TNF reset the hypothalamic set-point producing high fevers (often 38.5–40°C) and rigors.
Shaking chills accompany rapid temperature rise and are characteristic of bacteremic gram-negative urosepsis.
Cytokine-driven sympathetic activation and fever produce sinus tachycardia.
Compensatory tachypnea with metabolic acidosis and cytokine-driven respiratory drive.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Leukopenia in severe sepsis indicates poor prognosis.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Marrow neutrophil release; typical 12–25 ×10^9/L.
Left shift reflecting accelerated marrow neutrophil release.
Neutrophilic response to bacterial infection.
IL-6-driven hepatic acute-phase reactant; typical levels 100–300 mg/L; trends downward with effective therapy.
Bacterial-specific marker; rises rapidly with bacteremia and falls with effective antimicrobial therapy.
Cytokine-mediated malaise.
Cytokine-driven myalgia commonly accompanies bacteremic episodes.
Common sympathetic/cytokine-driven GI symptom; often limits oral intake and oral antibiotic feasibility.
Distributive vasodilation and capillary leak lower MAP; <65 mmHg defines vasopressor need.
qSOFA SBP cutoff ≤100 mmHg; component of severity scoring.
Tissue hypoperfusion and microcirculatory dysfunction; ≥2 mmol/L marks septic shock when accompanying vasopressor need.
Septic encephalopathy; one of qSOFA criteria.
Composite organ dysfunction score; ΔSOFA ≥2 defines sepsis.
Sepsis-related consumption and DIC.
Coagulopathy from consumption and hepatic dysfunction.
Lactic and AKI-related metabolic acidosis.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Most prominent in severe urosepsis with capillary leak / ARDS.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Sepsis-related lung injury reduces oxygenation.
Reduced GFR raises serum creatinine; KDIGO stages applied.
Reduced clearance and prerenal physiology raise BUN.
Oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/hr) in AKI; obstruction can produce anuria.
Reduced renal excretion; risk amplified by RAAS blockade.
Direct mapping to AKI event hazard.
Direct imaging finding of focal cavity with rim enhancement on CT/MRI.
Lesion size guides drainage decisions (commonly drainage if >3–5 cm or non-responsive).
Direct imaging finding indicating need for percutaneous or surgical drainage.
Greater extent (multiloculated, psoas extension) escalates source-control intensity.
Direct hazard mapping.
Direct hazard mapping.
Pathognomonic imaging finding of intraparenchymal gas on CT.
Huang–Tseng classification (1–4) stratifies extent and predicts mortality / nephrectomy need.
Direct event hazard.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Higher with Huang class 3B/4 or failed percutaneous drainage.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Nephrectomy is required when percutaneous drainage and antibiotics fail in fulminant disease.
Obstruction produces visible collecting-system dilation on US/CT.
Direct readout of obstructive contribution.
Defines obstructive pyelonephritis as a clinical entity requiring urgent decompression.
Obstruction mandates ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy.
Imaging shows ring shadow, cavitation, or sloughed papillae; can also be inferred from gross hematuria with passage of tissue.
Necrotic papillae produce gross or microscopic hematuria.
Sepsis with vasopressor requirement and lactate ≥2 mmol/L defines septic shock.
Severe urosepsis with ARDS or encephalopathy may require intubation.
Septic shock and multi-organ failure are dominant determinants of in-hospital mortality.
Historic mortality 40–80%; modern mortality 10–25% with prompt drainage.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Obstruction without timely decompression dramatically increases mortality.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Obstructive pyelonephritis without urgent drainage is the highest-acuity scenario in pyelonephritis.
Perinephric abscess undrained carries substantial mortality, especially in elderly/diabetic.
AKI requiring renal replacement therapy is independently associated with mortality.

mechanism_edges.conditionality: Pregnancy-specific; pyelonephritis complicates ~1–2% of pregnancies and is a leading cause of antepartum hospitalization.
mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Bacterial endotoxin and cytokines (notably IL-6) trigger uterine activity and preterm labor.
Obstruction proximal to ongoing infection produces pus-filled hydronephrosis (pyonephrosis), an absolute drainage indication.
Resistance lowers the prior that empiric therapy is active.
Direct readout.
Persistent fever and inflammatory markers beyond 72 h on appropriate antibiotics signal source-control failure.
Severe gram-negative urosepsis can trigger systemic coagulation activation and sepsis-induced DIC.
Severe systemic infection, shock, hypoxemia, ARDS, pulmonary edema, or fluid overload can increase oxygen or ventilatory support needs; this parallels the existing pao2_fio2_ratio pathway.

axes.shape_free_text: Acute spike to 38.5–40°C with rigors at presentation; defervesces over 48–72 h on appropriate therapy; persistent fever beyond 72 h suggests resistant organism, abscess, or undrained obstruction.
Sinus tachycardia 100–130 bpm during fever and bacteremia; resolves with sepsis control.
Tachypnea 20–28/min in moderate sepsis; >22/min meets qSOFA.
Falls in distributive urosepsis; <65 mmHg defines need for vasopressors.
qSOFA threshold ≤100 mmHg; severe shock <90 mmHg.
Usually preserved; falls in severe urosepsis with ARDS.

Oxygen or ventilatory support requirement: 0 room air, 1 low-flow nasal cannula, 2 mask or higher low-flow support, 3 high-flow nasal cannula, 4 noninvasive ventilation, 5 invasive ventilation or extracorporeal support.
Oliguria <0.5 mL/kg/hr in AKI; anuria suggests bilateral or solitary-kidney obstruction.
Shaking chills classically herald bacteremic spike at presentation.
Unilateral (occasionally bilateral) flank/loin pain; cardinal symptom distinguishing upper-tract from lower-tract UTI.
Costovertebral angle tenderness on percussion (Murphy's punch sign); typically unilateral.
Common; limits oral intake and oral antibiotic feasibility.
Lower-tract symptoms often precede or accompany pyelonephritis but may be absent in 30–40%.
Lower-tract irritative symptoms; often present at onset.
Generalized lower abdominal pain occasionally dominates and mimics intra-abdominal pathology.
Confusion/delirium especially in elderly with urosepsis; often the dominant presenting feature.
Cytokine-driven malaise that often persists 1–2 weeks into convalescence.
Diffuse myalgias in bacteremic episodes.
Microscopic hematuria common; gross hematuria suggests papillary necrosis or hemorrhagic cystitis component.
Leukocytosis typically 12–25 ×10^9/L; leukopenia <4 in severe sepsis carries worse prognosis.
Neutrophilia drives the leukocytosis.
Left shift; bands often >0.10 in active bacteremic infection.
Falls modestly in severe sepsis; <100 ×10^9/L suggests DIC.
Rises quickly to 100–300 mg/L; lags fever by 12–24 h; declines with adequate therapy with half-life ~3–5 days.
Bacterial-specific marker; often >2 ng/mL in bacteremic pyelonephritis, >10 ng/mL in septic shock; falls rapidly with effective therapy.
Rises in AKI from sepsis or obstruction; reversibility depends on prompt source control.
Rises with prerenal physiology and AKI; disproportionately elevated relative to creatinine in dehydration.
≥2 mmol/L suggests sepsis; ≥4 mmol/L heralds shock and triggers aggressive resuscitation.
Rises in AKI and metabolic acidosis.
Often mildly low from SIADH-like physiology or dehydration with replacement.
Decreases with lactic and AKI-related metabolic acidosis.
Mild prolongation in sepsis; marked prolongation suggests DIC.
Negative acute-phase reactant; falls during acute inflammation.
Decreases in severe urosepsis with capillary leak / ARDS; <300 indicates ALI/ARDS.
Composite organ dysfunction score; ΔSOFA ≥2 from baseline defines sepsis.
Marked pyuria typical (≥10 WBC/HPF); near-universal in pyelonephritis. Absent pyuria in obstructed pyelonephritis can occur if obstructed kidney does not communicate with bladder urine.
Positive in nitrate-reducing Enterobacterales; negative in Enterococcus, Staph saprophyticus, Pseudomonas, dilute urine.
Surrogate for pyuria; near-universally positive.
Highly specific for upper-tract source; insensitive (~30%).
≥10^5 CFU/mL midstream (≥10^4 in catheter samples); reduced if antibiotic exposure preceded sampling.
Typically 10^5–10^8 CFU/mL.
Predominantly E. coli; positive Gram stain on uncentrifuged urine correlates with high bacterial load.
Most common pathogen (~70–85% community, 50–60% healthcare-associated).
Higher in healthcare-associated, instrumented, and catheter-associated cases; intrinsic cephalosporin resistance.
Region-dependent; typically 5–15% community, up to 30–50% healthcare-associated.
Positive in 15–30% of hospitalized acute pyelonephritis.
Often low-grade bacteremia (<10 CFU/mL) but can be high in obstructive disease.
Pyelonephritis is the leading source of community-acquired gram-negative bacteremia.
Concentric urothelial wall thickening on contrast CT or US; supports upper-tract diagnosis.
Reflects active capsular/perinephric edema.
Wedge-shaped delayed enhancement on contrast CT; classic radiologic sign.
Focal hypoenhancement on arterial-phase CT; spectrum includes acute focal bacterial nephritis (lobar nephronia).
Renal cortical or corticomedullary abscess on CT/MRI.
Drives drainage decisions: <3 cm often resolves with antibiotics alone, 3–5 cm percutaneous drainage often required, >5 cm strongly favors drainage.
Perinephric/Gerota's space abscess; almost always requires drainage.
Multiloculated extension into psoas, retroperitoneum, or contralateral side intensifies management.
Intraparenchymal/perinephric gas on CT; pathognomonic.
Class 1: gas in collecting system; 2: parenchymal gas no extension; 3A: perinephric extension; 3B: pararenal extension; 4: bilateral or solitary kidney.
SFU grading 0–4; grade ≥3 with infection mandates urgent drainage.
Obstructing ureteral calculus is the most common surgical cause of obstructive pyelonephritis.
Struvite stones with chronic infection; classic substrate for xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis.
Chronic destructive granulomatous variant typically with staghorn calculus and non-functioning kidney; usually requires nephrectomy.
Ring shadow / cavitary papilla on CT urography; risk factors include diabetes, sickle cell, NSAID/analgesic use.
Pus-filled hydronephrosis; absolute indication for urgent decompression.
Dominant source category for pyelonephritis-related bacteremia.
Mechanical obstruction component requiring drainage.
Obstructive pyelonephritis = pyelonephritis + urinary obstruction; surgical/urologic emergency.
Need for drainage (stent / nephrostomy / abscess drainage / nephrectomy).
Quality of source control achieved; low values predict treatment failure regardless of antibiotic choice.
Adequacy of decompression by ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy.
Indwelling urinary catheter as source/contributor.
Presence of indwelling urinary catheter; raises resistance and Enterococcus probability.
History of stones increases obstructive risk and recurrence.
Predisposes to recurrent ascending infection and renal scarring.
Spinal cord injury / MS / diabetic cystopathy; predisposes via incomplete emptying and instrumentation.
Recent ureteroscopy, stent, or surgery raises healthcare-associated and resistant pathogen probability.
Antibiotic use within 90 days raises ESBL/quinolone-resistance probability and may obscure cultures.
Glycemic burden (especially HbA1c >9% / glucose >250) is the dominant risk factor for emphysematous pyelonephritis and papillary necrosis.

Pregnancy contraindicates fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines, and TMP-SMX (avoided in 1st and late 3rd trimester); right-sided pyelonephritis predominates due to dextrorotation; complicates 1–2% of pregnancies.
Diabetes, transplant, neutropenia, advanced HIV; raises bacteremia and complication risk.
Risk score from prior ESBL colonization, recent antibiotics, healthcare exposure, regional prevalence; drives empiric escalation to carbapenem.
Healthcare exposure, structural urinary disease, indwelling catheter, prior Pseudomonas; drives anti-pseudomonal coverage choice.
Risk of CRE; drives ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam, or imipenem-relebactam choice.
Probability that the organism is carbapenem-susceptible; near-universally true for ESBL Enterobacterales without CRE risk.
Region-dependent; commonly 80–95% for community E. coli pyelonephritis without ESBL risk.
Active against most non-ESBL Enterobacterales and Pseudomonas; reduced reliability for ESBL urosepsis.
Permitted in non-pregnant adults without QTc/aneurysm/tendinopathy concerns and in regions where local resistance <10–20%.
Limited by AKI, age, and ototoxicity; brief courses acceptable as adjunct or in pregnancy.
Modulates β-lactam choice; cross-reactivity with cephalosporins low (<2%) for most penicillin allergies.
Anaphylaxis or SJS history; contraindicates β-lactams broadly.
Probability current empiric regimen covers the actual organism.
Initial inactive empiric coverage drives delayed source control and rising mortality.
Adjustments required for β-lactams, fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides as creatinine clearance falls.
Persistent fever, leukocytosis, or pain beyond 72 h on appropriate antibiotics; mandates re-imaging for abscess/obstruction.
Highest in the first 1–3 days; drops with adequate antibiotics + source control.
Affects ~10–25% of hospitalized pyelonephritis; reversible with source control and sepsis resolution.
Required mainly in severe urosepsis with ARDS or encephalopathy.
Rises after 48–72 h of inadequate therapy; falls quickly once organism-active antibiotics start.
Higher with diabetes, obstruction, delayed therapy.
Predominantly in poorly controlled diabetes; carries 10–25% modern mortality.
Highly conditional on obstruction; surgical emergency.
Indicated for refractory emphysematous pyelonephritis (Huang 3B/4 failing drainage), XGP, and uncontrolled sepsis from a non-functioning kidney.
Pregnancy-specific; minimized by prompt antibiotics and tocolysis when needed.
Long-tail recurrence risk in patients with persistent obstruction, reflux, neurogenic bladder, or untreated nephrolithiasis.
Overall in-hospital mortality 1–3% in uncomplicated, rises to 10–25% with septic shock or emphysematous disease, higher with delayed source control. Hazard concentrated in the first 7 days.
Probability that the urinary pathogen is susceptible to ciprofloxacin/levofloxacin; determined by urine or blood culture susceptibility, not by symptoms alone.
Probability that the urinary pathogen is susceptible to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole; used for definitive oral step-down when known susceptible.
Hazard of sepsis-induced disseminated intravascular coagulation in severe urosepsis; tracks thrombocytopenia, prolonged PT/INR, fibrinogen/FDP/D-dimer abnormalities, and shock severity.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Each 1°C rise correlates with ~10 bpm increase in heart rate; residual covariance after the cytokine mechanism is accounted for.
Hypoperfusion drives anaerobic metabolism; residual covariance beyond shared sepsis driver.
Oliguria leads creatinine rise by 12–48 h.
Persistent fever beyond 72 h on adequate antibiotics is the canonical clinical signal that an abscess or undrained collection is forming.
Unrelieved obstruction quickly converts pus-containing collecting system into pyonephrosis.
Uncontrolled diabetes is present in >90% of emphysematous pyelonephritis cases.
Falling platelets and rising INR co-move in sepsis-related coagulopathy / DIC.
Falling clearance increases need for dose adjustment of renally cleared antibiotics.
Risk score predicts the actual organism resistance status.
Each hour of delay in active therapy increases mortality in septic shock; more pronounced in elderly/diabetic.
Failure to relieve obstruction or drain abscess is the dominant non-antibiotic determinant of mortality.
Hazard activates only when the patient is pregnant.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Effective against most community E. coli/Klebsiella/Proteus.
ESBL Enterobacterales hydrolyze ceftriaxone; carbapenem required.
Enterococcus is intrinsically resistant; needs ampicillin or vancomycin coverage.
Ceftriaxone has no antipseudomonal activity.
Antibiotics alone cannot resolve obstruction or drain abscess.
Anaphylaxis history precludes use.

treatments.context_specific_role: First-line empiric IV agent for community-acquired acute pyelonephritis without ESBL or pseudomonal risk; suitable in pregnancy.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Anti-pseudomonal coverage important in healthcare-associated/instrumented disease.
Variable activity vs ESBL; often inadequate for severe bacteremic ESBL.
Same as other antibiotics.

side_effects.interpretation: Cefepime neurotoxicity in renal failure / overdose; encephalopathy, myoclonus, NCSE.

treatments.context_specific_role: Empiric coverage when pseudomonal risk is elevated (healthcare-associated, indwelling devices, recent instrumentation).

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Covers Pseudomonas and most non-ESBL Enterobacterales plus enterococci.
MERINO trial data caution against piperacillin-tazobactam for ESBL bacteremia.

side_effects.interpretation: Possible AKI signal especially when combined with vancomycin.

treatments.context_specific_role: Empiric alternative in healthcare-associated pyelonephritis with pseudomonal and enterococcal concern.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Carbapenems are the first-line definitive therapy for ESBL Enterobacterales bacteremia.
CRE require ceftazidime-avibactam, meropenem-vaborbactam, or imipenem-relebactam.
Severe penicillin/cephalosporin reactions broadly preclude carbapenem use.

side_effects.interpretation: Reduced seizure threshold (lower with meropenem vs imipenem).

treatments.context_specific_role: Empiric for severe sepsis/septic shock with high ESBL probability or known ESBL colonization; definitive for confirmed ESBL.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Fluoroquinolones work well for pyelonephritis only when the organism is susceptible.
Good oral bioavailability and renal tissue penetration make this useful for outpatient therapy or step-down when eligible.
Generally avoided in pregnancy when safer beta-lactam options are available.
Recent fluoroquinolone or broad antibiotic exposure increases resistance probability.
Obstruction, pyonephrosis, or abscess will not be cured by oral therapy alone.

side_effects.interpretation: CNS toxicity risk, especially in older adults or renal impairment.

treatments.context_specific_role: Oral or IV option for susceptible pyelonephritis; useful as step-down after initial IV therapy or outpatient therapy when local resistance and patient context permit.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: TMP-SMX is appropriate for pyelonephritis only when susceptibility is known or very likely.
Renal dose adjustment and potassium monitoring are required when kidney function is impaired.
Avoid near term and use cautiously in pregnancy depending on trimester and alternatives.

failure_modes: severe renal impairment with hyperkalemia risk

side_effects.interpretation: Trimethoprim can raise potassium, especially in CKD or ACEi/ARB exposure.
Can increase creatinine by tubular secretion inhibition without true GFR fall, and can also contribute to AKI in susceptible patients.

treatments.context_specific_role: Definitive oral step-down for susceptible organisms; not a reliable empiric choice when resistance is common.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Useful as a one-time high-concentration gram-negative kill adjunct when renal and ototoxicity risks are acceptable.
AKI or CKD sharply narrows the therapeutic window.

side_effects.interpretation: Dose- and exposure-dependent nephrotoxicity; avoid prolonged therapy when possible.

treatments.context_specific_role: One-time adjunct at presentation in severe pyelonephritis or local resistance settings; not preferred as prolonged monotherapy.

treatments.drug: Ampicillin or Vancomycin for Enterococcus coverage

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Enterococcus coverage is useful when Enterococcus is isolated or strongly suspected from catheter/instrumentation context.
Ampicillin is avoided with immediate beta-lactam hypersensitivity; vancomycin may be used when appropriate.
Both ampicillin and vancomycin require renal adjustment; vancomycin exposure requires monitoring.

failure_modes: ordinary E. coli pyelonephritis without Enterococcus

side_effects.interpretation: Vancomycin exposure can worsen AKI risk, especially with other nephrotoxins.

treatments.context_specific_role: Add-on or definitive therapy for Enterococcus pyelonephritis, especially catheter-associated or post-instrumentation cases.

treatments.drug: Urgent urinary decompression (ureteral stent or percutaneous nephrostomy)

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Decompression directly relieves obstructed infected urine, the causal source-control problem.
Mortality benefit is largest when source control is initially inadequate.

failure_modes: no obstruction or drainable collecting-system source

push_targets.clinical_rationale: Shock physiology improves only after infected obstruction is relieved, alongside fluids/vasopressors.

treatments.context_specific_role: Definitive emergency source control for obstructive pyelonephritis or pyonephrosis; antibiotics alone are insufficient.

treatments.drug: Percutaneous renal or perinephric abscess drainage

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Collections above roughly 3-5 cm or persistent fever usually require drainage.
Drainage only helps when there is a drainable focus.

treatments.context_specific_role: Source control for renal or perinephric abscess, especially persistent fever after 48-72 h of active antibiotics or collection larger than 3-5 cm.

treatments.drug: Nephrectomy for refractory non-salvageable infected kidney

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Modern nephrectomy is reserved for extensive emphysematous or necrotic infection failing drainage/antibiotics.
Persistent clinical nonresponse despite active antibiotics and attempted drainage suggests a refractory septic focus.

failure_modes: salvageable kidney responding to percutaneous drainage
bilateral disease or solitary kidney where nephron preservation is critical

side_effects.interpretation: Loss of renal mass can reduce long-term kidney function, especially with CKD or solitary kidney.

treatments.context_specific_role: Rare last-resort source control for refractory emphysematous pyelonephritis, xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis, or a non-functioning infected kidney.

present.trajectory_modulation: Higher baseline risk because of shorter urethra and ascending infection; uncomplicated presentations common in younger women.
Higher risk from urinary stasis and reflux; increases hospitalization threshold, preterm labor hazard, and narrows antibiotic choices.

poor_control.trajectory_modulation: Raises bacteremia, AKI, renal abscess, papillary necrosis, and emphysematous pyelonephritis risk.

present.trajectory_modulation: Converts infection into obstructive pyelonephritis/pyonephrosis; makes decompression a source-control treatment rather than optional support.
Raises Enterococcus, Pseudomonas, polymicrobial, and resistant-organism probability.
Raises recurrent and bilateral upper-tract infection risk.
Stasis and catheter exposure increase recurrence and resistant pathogen probability.
May blunt fever/WBC response while increasing bacteremia, abscess, fungal, and severe sepsis risk.
Raises AKI consequence and renal-dose constraints; obstruction is higher-stakes in solitary kidney.
Raises ESBL/AmpC/fluoroquinolone resistance and initial inactive therapy risk.

over_65.trajectory_modulation: More atypical presentation, delirium, bacteremia, AKI, and septic shock; flank pain may be muted.

present.trajectory_modulation: Pyelonephritis in men often implies complicated urinary tract anatomy, prostatitis, obstruction, or instrumentation.

supportive_care: Obtain urinalysis, urine culture, and susceptibility before antibiotics when feasible; do not delay antibiotics in sepsis.
Obtain blood cultures in hospitalized, septic, obstructed, pregnant, immunocompromised, or healthcare-associated presentations.
Assess for obstruction or abscess with renal ultrasound or CT when severe illness, AKI, stone history, persistent fever beyond 48-72 h, or treatment nonresponse is present.
Early IV fluids for sepsis physiology; monitor MAP, lactate, urine output, creatinine, and electrolytes.
Norepinephrine for septic shock after adequate fluid resuscitation, targeting MAP at least 65 mmHg unless individualized otherwise.
Analgesia and antipyretics while avoiding nephrotoxins when AKI risk is high.
Renal-dose adjust beta-lactams, fluoroquinolones, TMP-SMX, aminoglycosides, and vancomycin according to kidney function.
Avoid nitrofurantoin and fosfomycin as treatment for pyelonephritis because renal parenchymal levels are inadequate.
Pregnancy: admit for initial IV beta-lactam therapy, fetal/obstetric assessment when indicated, and avoid fluoroquinolones/TMP-SMX when safer alternatives fit the clinical context.
If obstruction, pyonephrosis, or infected stone is suspected, involve urology urgently for stent or nephrostomy; antibiotics alone are not adequate source control.
If abscess is suspected or fever persists despite active therapy, repeat imaging and consider percutaneous drainage based on size, location, and clinical response.
Monitor for DIC, ARDS, AKI, encephalopathy, and recurrent fever in severe urosepsis.
